[...] [p. 279] Legbó has three tonemes as can be shown for nouns as follows: [...] [p. 280] Stress. Stress is not phonemic. Two factors control the distribution of stress within the word: (1) Tone: the stress is born by the syllable with the highest tone. (2) Linear position in the word: out of several syllables with the same height of tone the one nearest to the end of the word bears the stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Legbo is a three-tone language (H, M, L). Word stress is non-contrastive and fully predictable from tone: within the phonological word (1-6 syllables), stress falls on the syllable bearing the highest tone; if several syllables tie for highest tone, the rightmost of them (nearest the word end) is stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the authors note that mid tone and stress are not marked in their transcription (p. 256). A separate word-level 'tenseness' feature (fortis, lengthened consonant with compensatory vowel shortening) is phonemic but is treated apart from stress (pp. 280-282).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word ('stress group', 1-6 syllables, potential pause on either side), which 'largely corresponds to the word unit in the grammatical hierarchy' (p. 257). Utterance-level prominence (raised first syllable, decrescendo, final pitch drop) is described separately (pp. 257-258). Description is of the Adadama dialect, fieldwork 1964-66.
new_statements.identity_note: Spreda & Spreda (1966) call the language 'Legbó' and the people/clan 'Agbó' (= Glottolog legb1242 Legbo, ISO agb, also spelled Leggbo in Hyman/Udoh/Paster's work); their statement explicitly describes the Adadama dialect (one of four township dialects: Igbo Ekureku, Igbo Imabana, Adadama, Itigidi; Glottolog lists no subdialect codes). The Hyman/Udoh/Paster materials are based on Imelda Udoh as consultant (Berkeley field methods 2001-02).

sources.note: p. 257: the word is defined as the stress-bearing unit (stress group); p. 280 (sec. X Suprasegmental Features, 'Stress'): stress is not phonemic; it falls on the syllable with the highest tone, and among syllables of equal tone height on the one nearest the end of the word. Three tonemes H/M/L. Also a word-level 'tenseness' (fortis/long consonant) feature. Dialect: Adadama.
